title: Russians go to polls against backdrop of Ukraine war and Putin’s tightening grip
author: Pjotr Sauer
content:
Russians are going to the polls to elect a new State Duma in a tightly controlled vote stripped of meaningful competition and with little doubt about the result.
Vladimir Putin’s United Russia is expected to extend the grip on parliament it has held for 23 years, alongside a handful of nominal opposition parties that reliably vote with the Kremlin on the issues that matter. The three-day vote begins on Friday, with results expected after polls close on Sunday.
For all the predictability of the outcome, the first Duma election since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 is taking place against the backdrop of a war that, once distant for many Russians, is increasingly intruding into everyday life.
Swarms of Ukrainian drones have struck oil refineries, factories and logistics hubs across Russia over the summer, while polling has pointed to growing anxiety about the course of the fighting and what may still lie ahead.
Against that backdrop, the Kremlin has tightened its grip further.
Last month, the authorities barred Yabloko, the liberal anti-war party, from the ballot, removing the only political force remaining in Russia that was openly challenging the invasion of Ukraine.
That leaves a handful of other parties, from the Communists to the far-right Liberal Democrats, which together form what is known in Russia as the “systemic opposition”: groups permitted to criticise the authorities at the margins, but which fall into line with United Russia on issues that matter to the Kremlin.
![A Russian Communist party rally in downtown Moscow on Thursday.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/93e557feff307c024a540382f44898a3e69faaf7/0_0_6000_4000/master/6000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
For years, they have served as a political safety valve, giving voters somewhere to register discontent without posing a serious threat to the ruling party’s dominance. But even by the diminished standards of Russian politics, these parliamentary campaigns have been strikingly lifeless.
“In most elections, candidates compete for attention. In Russia this year, many are doing the opposite,” said Farida Rustamova, a political analyst and founder of the independent Vlast newsletter. “No one wants to come into the spotlight or discuss anything sensitive.”
Most candidates have barely campaigned at all, she noted.
Televised debates have at times taken place in half-empty studios because politicians failed to turn up, producing awkward clips that quickly became memes online.
![A campaign worker handing out promotional materials for United Russia in Yaroslavl.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/ea833a95b77d78c716a627c2dfd117ae5f37b603/0_0_6657_4718/master/6657.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
United Russia’s campaign videos have leaned heavily on low-budget AI, with few memorable slogans or promises. None of the parties has dared to address the growing questions surrounding the continuing war that increasingly dominate private conversations.
“The Kremlin is deliberately keeping the election low-key, as greater interest would not benefit them. They don’t want to discuss difficult issues and just [want to] get it over with,” said a person close to the Kremlin, speaking on condition of anonymity.
after newsletter promotion
By keeping the election subdued, Moscow hoped to depress turnout among disaffected and independent-minded voters while ensuring its own supporters made it to the polls, said Rustamova.
Yabloko’s exclusion followed the same logic.
Several observers believe that officials had initially expected the party to receive a negligible result, demonstrating how little support remained for an explicitly anti-war platform. But when polling instead suggested growing support for the party, the authorities removed it from the ballot rather than risk an unscripted result.
![Young woman handing out flyers](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/276e3522434840702d0a3efd2e75948d005b2507/0_0_6524_4532/master/6524.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Vladimir Gelman, a professor of Russian politics at the University of Helsinki, said another purpose of the elections was to provide the Kremlin with a continuing source of legitimacy and reinforce the impression that there was broad public consent behind the political system and the war.
“Even though these elections are neither free nor fair, they are still the only source of legitimacy,” he said.
In a televised address before the vote this week, Putin explicitly linked participation in the election to the war in Ukraine, presenting voting as a demonstration of unity in the face of outside pressure.
“Your choice and your will will once again demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our soldiers, that we are a united people bound together by shared values, historical memory and love for our homeland,” Putin said.
Putin himself secured another six-year term in the 2024 presidential election, with genuine opposition barred from the ballot, extending his rule until at least 2030.
![Putin sitting at a table in front of a Russia flag](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/4c461f4fd4f4c9c8ddc88956e4f9445b0c878f87/0_0_3428_2286/master/3428.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
For many Russians, however, the election’s greater significance lies not in the result, but in what follows.
With Moscow’s troops making little progress at high cost in Ukraine, rumours of another large-scale mobilisation have spread across the country. The fear is that once the election is safely out of the way and a compliant new Duma is installed, the Kremlin will have greater freedom to pursue unpopular measures it has so far avoided.
The anxiety has already prompted some young men to leave the country, hoping to wait out any new mobilisation – scenes that carry echoes of September 2022, when hundreds of thousands of Russians fled after Putin announced the first wartime draft.
The person close to the Kremlin said several friends had sent their sons abroad in recent weeks, a sign, he said, that even among those with access to the system, few are certain what will happen after the voting.
Putin has sought to calm those fears. In recent weeks, he has twice dismissed suggestions that a new mobilisation is imminent.
But those reassurances have not been enough for some men, including Dmitry, who flew to Yerevan, Armenia last week. “I’ll just wait a few weeks after the elections,” he said, adding that he felt the risk of a new mobilisation was too high to ignore. “Let’s see if anything changes after the vote.”
summary: Russians are voting in a tightly controlled State Duma election stripped of meaningful competition, with Vladimir Putin's United Russia expected to easily maintain its parliamentary dominance. The three-day vote is taking place against the backdrop of the ongoing war in Ukraine, increasing domestic anxiety, and a deliberate Kremlin strategy to keep the election low-key and subdue turnout among independent voters. The liberal anti-war party Yabloko was barred from the ballot, and remaining parties have largely avoided campaigning on sensitive issues. Many citizens fear that once the election concludes, the Kremlin may pursue unpopular measures such as a new large-scale military mobilization.
key_points: Vladimir Putin's United Russia is widely expected to extend its 23-year grip on the State Duma.
The liberal anti-war party Yabloko was barred from the ballot by authorities ahead of the vote.
The Kremlin deliberately kept the election subdued to depress turnout among disaffected voters and avoid discussing the war.
Putin linked participation in the election to the war in Ukraine, presenting the vote as a demonstration of national unity.
Many Russians fear that a new large-scale military mobilization will be announced after the election is completed.

title: Trump administration approves sale of F-35 jets to Saudi Arabia
author: Al Jazeera Staff
content:
![LAKENHEATH, ENGLAND - APRIL 08: A US-AF F-35 Lightning II stealth multirole fighter jet overflies RAF Lakenheath on April 08, 2026 in Lakenheath, England. Keir Starmer has pledged to deny the US permission to use British sovereign bases, including RAF Lakenheath for offensive operations against Iranian infrastructure. While limited access for defensive missions was previously approved, the UK has drawn a firm line against strikes targeting civilian facilities. Over the weekend President Donald Trump issued a "final warning" to Iran, threatening a massive four-hour "obliteration" of its civilian infrastructure if the Strait of Hormuz is not reopened by his deadline of 20:00 eastern time today. (Photo by Leon Neal/Getty Images)](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/getty_6a4de7b5a6-1783490485.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
United States President Donald Trump’s administration has asked lawmakers to clear the sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia for an estimated $24.3bn.
“This proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a major non-NATO ally that is a force for political stability and economic progress in the Gulf region,” the State Department said in a statement on Thursday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Fighting continues between Yemen gov’t forces, Houthis: What is the latest?
- list 2 of 3Saudi Arabia promises to respond to Houthi attacks ‘firmly’
- list 3 of 3Five killed as Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis trade attacks
The administration said the sale of the jets, the most advanced fighter aircraft the US has, would “not alter the military balance in the region” in keeping with longstanding US policy that Israel must have a military edge over potential regional adversaries.
The announcement comes after the Houthis in Yemen claimed on Wednesday they shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet over Marib, a key city in their battle against Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces. The group released video of fighters in the city standing before burning wreckage of what appeared to be a US-made F-15 fighter jet with Saudi Arabian markings.
The Houthis claim the aircraft was shot down with a “locally made” surface-to-air missile, which would mark a dramatic change in the group’s ability to wage war in the area. Until now, Saudi Arabia’s military has enjoyed relative air superiority in Yemen, and has relied heavily on its ability to carry out air strikes in the neighbouring country.
Intensifying fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis reportedly killed at least five people, including three children, on Thursday.
Saudi Arabia has unsuccessfully sought to have Washington play a more direct role in the kingdom’s conflict with Houthi forces. The US has said it will not directly intervene in the conflict between the Iran-backed Houthis, Saudi Arabia, and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.
Chinese concerns
Washington also has concerns about potential Chinese espionage related to the jets.
The New York Times reported this week that US intelligence analysts have raised the possibility that Beijing could acquire F-35 technology through its partnerships with Riyadh.
US congressional Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi, a Democratic member of the House Intelligence Committee, expressed opposition to the sale on those grounds.
The deal should not go ahead “when our own intelligence community is warning that it could put the crown jewels of American military technology within reach of the Chinese Communist Party,” Krishnamoorthi said in a statement.
Saudi Arabia signed a mutual defense agreement, dubbed the Mecca Agreement, with Pakistan and Turkiye last month, a sign the countries are seeking ways to provide for mutual defence that relies less on Washington.
Saudi Arabia has long sought to buy F-35s, but officials from Israel – the only country in the region with the fighter jets – have voiced concern about their sale to Riyadh despite a push for the kingdom to normalise relations. Turkiye, a NATO member that took part in a multi-country development of the F-35 jets, has been barred from receiving the aircraft since 2019 after it purchased anti-aircraft missiles from Russia.
summary: The Trump administration has asked lawmakers to approve the sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia for an estimated $24.3bn. The State Department stated the deal supports US foreign policy and national security objectives without altering the regional military balance. However, the proposed sale faces opposition from US lawmakers over potential risks of Chinese espionage and technology transfer. The announcement also follows recent Houthi claims of shooting down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet in Yemen amid intensifying fighting.
key_points: The Trump administration asked Congress to clear a $24.3bn sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia.
The State Department maintained that the sale will not alter the region's military balance, preserving Israel's qualitative edge.
US intelligence analysts and lawmakers raised concerns that Saudi partnerships could allow Beijing to acquire sensitive F-35 technology.
The announcement coincided with intensifying conflict in Yemen, where Houthi forces recently claimed to have shot down a Saudi F-15 jet.

title: Why Canadians are ready for closer ties with Europe
author: Robin Levinson-King
content:
Watch: 'A better opportunity' - Canadians on a closer alliance with Europe
- Published
Miriam Levin-Gold likes Prime Minister Mark Carney's idea of Canadians being able to live and work in the European Union under proposed closer ties with the trade bloc.
"I think that's great for young people to explore different parts of the world and work in different places and have different experiences," the commuter told the BBC in Toronto.
Canadians woke up to news of Carney's speech to the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Thursday morning, welcoming the EU's ambition for Canada to become its first "associate member" as he urged closer co-operation on defence and energy.
"We should deepen our people-to-people ties, allowing our youth to live, work and study where they want on either side of the Atlantic," the PM said.
Carney told MEPs that Canada and Europe were "stronger together" in the face of "geopolitical rupture".
![Miriam Levin-Gold holds a microphone](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/8c43/live/071e0fd0-b2c8-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.jpg)
Miriam Levin-Gold is excited about potentially greater opportunities for young Canadians to be able to explore the EU
But before Canadians start packing their bags - "associate member" status does not currently exist within the EU and could take years to implement, given that all 27 EU member states would have to approve such an arrangement.
Nevertheless, people the BBC spoke to were excited about the potential prospect of working and studying in the EU as news of Carney's speech spread.
Alex Nash, from Montreal, said closer ties would clear away the obstacles of work visas and permits.
"It would certainly be really nice for that to be easier, more convenient and to be able to visit more easily," she said.
Canadian social media has lit up with the topic.
One person on a Facebook group, A Canadian Outlook, said they would love the opportunity for their grandchildren to study at European universities for better rates. Another woman said it would make it much easier for the home she already owns in France.
"Snow birds are going to love it," another person said, referring to Canadians who head to warmer locations for winter.
The sentiments hint at dissatisfaction in Canada over bilateral tensions with the US.
Watch: Is Canada about to join the EU?
Growing up in Canada, David Jardine thought of the US as not just a neighbour, but an epicentre of culture and cool.
"I remember wanting to go and visit New York all the time," he told the BBC after finishing his overnight shift, not far from one of Toronto's most iconic buildings, the CN tower.
But he's become a lot more sceptical in the light of US President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada and rhetoric about annexation.
"I would say I think not only does it make more sense to associate closely with Europe, it's a place that I would rather be associating with given the way things are these days," he said.
![Two people hold microphones and give an interview](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/9169/live/94866990-b2a9-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.jpg)
David Jardine and Alex Nash hope Carney's news means there will be fewer obstacles to spending time in Europe
Maggie Stainton, who manages local pub C'est What in Toronto's St Lawrence Market district, became emotional when she spoke about Canada's frayed ties with the US.
"It's too volatile with the United States," she said. "I feel that there's some stability in Europe."
For decades, America has been a cultural centre of gravity that is difficult to avoid, with many Canadian actors working in Hollywood and Canadian radio stations playing US music.
"I think we're forced to feel more American simply by the influences that we have," Stainton added.
"However, I think deep down, I definitely I lean towards feeling more European in my ideas and ideals."
These views were echoed by many other people the BBC spoke to in the centre of Canada's biggest city.
Carney, who used to lead Canada and Britain's central banks, was elected on a promise that he would not only take a tough stance against Trump, but broaden Canada's economic horizons.
Up to 72% of Canadian exports are to the US, and the ongoing trade tensions have spurred Ottawa to seek closer ties with other nations.
![A woman holds a microphone and speaks to a reporter](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/a004/live/a5ecc210-b2a9-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.jpg)
Maggie Stainton is disappointed by the frayed relationship with the US
The EU, in many ways, would seem a natural fit. Over half of Canada's population reported having European origins, according to the last census, which was taken in 2021.
A recent Abacus Data survey conducted before Carney's speech found that 80% of Canadians say the country should deepen strategic cooperation with the EU, and over half feel closer to Europe than America.
However, details of Carney's proposed plans for greater ties with the EU are scarce.
A pair of opposition Conservative MPs have called on him to elaborate on what he and the bloc plan to work towards.
"It could be a concrete, meaningful proposal. Or it could be just words and vibes," said Adam Chambers, MP for Simcoe North in Ontario, during an interview with the BBC on the eve of Carney's speech on Thursday.
Chambers alluded to the existing Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (Ceta) between the EU and Canada, highlighting that it still awaits ratification by multiple EU nations.
![A man holds a microphone and gives an interview](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1680/cpsprodpb/797f/live/69c867d0-b2cc-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.jpg)
Ahmed Khalil hopes ties with Europe brings in more money to Canada in light of tensions with the US
And while deepening ties with Europe would be welcomed by many Canadians, there is still a sense that the country's relationship with the US - however strained - must not crumble.
"I grew up here. I've been here 40 years in Canada, in Ontario, and America's always been the neighbour," says Ahmed Khalil.
Building bridges with Europe makes sense, he said: "I think it brings in more money for Canada and more culture, brings Europeans over, probably solves a lot of problems."
But Canada shouldn't forget its southern neighbour, added Khalil.
"I think both are equally valuable to us," he said. "Both are equally valid."
With additional reporting by Madeline Halpert and James FitzGerald
summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney proposed closer ties with the European Union during a speech in Strasbourg, suggesting Canada become an EU "associate member" with shared defence, energy, and freedom of movement. Many Canadians have welcomed the idea, expressing excitement over potential opportunities to live, work, and study in Europe. This shift in sentiment also reflects growing dissatisfaction and trade tensions with the United States. However, experts note that "associate member" status does not currently exist and would require approval from all 27 EU member states, meaning implementation could take years.
key_points: Prime Minister Mark Carney urged closer cooperation with the EU, proposing that Canada become its first "associate member."
The proposal includes allowing youth on both sides of the Atlantic to live, work, and study freely.
Many Canadians reacted positively, citing enthusiasm for easier travel and reduced visa obstacles, as well as frustration over volatile US trade tensions.
An "associate member" status does not currently exist in the EU and would require unanimous approval from all 27 member states, potentially taking years to implement.
Opposition MPs have called on Carney to provide concrete details regarding the proposed plans, noting that existing agreements like Ceta still await full ratification.

title: Serial killer fears in Johannesburg after ninth body found
author: Ben Farmer
content:
![Crime scene investigators examine the area in Dawn Park where the latest murder victim was found](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/17/TELEMMGLPICT000503393980_17896375074230_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqA7N2CxnJWnYI3tCbVBgu9T0aesusvN1TE7a0ddd_esI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Crime scene investigators examine the area in Dawn Park where the latest murder victim was found](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/17/TELEMMGLPICT000503393980_17896375074230_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqA7N2CxnJWnYI3tCbVBgu9T0aesusvN1TE7a0ddd_esI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Residents east of Johannesburg fear a serial killer may be at large after the body of a ninth woman was discovered near the city.
All the victims have been found in the Ekurhuleni municipality, with seven of the bodies discovered since the start of this month.
Police in South Africa have stressed that they have not established whether the deaths are connected or if it is the work of a serial killer.
The deaths have shocked a country that suffers from a high murder rate and a long record of violence against women.
Police have set up checkpoints in the municipality and will lock down the Kempton Park area, where several bodies have been found.
“We cannot continue picking up bodies,” Tebello Mosikili, the deputy police chief, told reporters in Dawn Park, where the latest body was found at the side of a road on Thursday morning.
![Police guard the crime scene in Dawn Park after residents flocked to the area](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/17/TELEMMGLPICT000503394087_17896375188981_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwfSVWeZ_vEN7c6bHu2jJnT8.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The unidentified ninth victim was about 30 years of age and was found near a building site with her throat cut and an apparent stab wound to her side.
Police said the latest discovery “will be added to the investigations into the deaths of women in Ekurhuleni”.
Earlier this week, Fred Kekana, the Gauteng provincial commissioner, said: “Police are comparing the evidence, timelines, locations, victim profiles and circumstances of each case before reaching conclusions.
“While investigations are still under way and the South African Police Service has not, at this stage, confirmed that the deaths are linked to a serial killer, the similarities are sufficiently concerning for the police to issue a public warning and intensify investigations.”
All the victims have been young women, aged between 20 and 38, and have been found either naked or partially clothed with bruises on their bodies.
![The scene in Dawn Park where a woman's body was discovered on Thursday morning](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/09/17/TELEMMGLPICT000503394480_17896375183730_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq9k_NRcUxd_vb3GsOEtUiIv4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The first body was found on July 17, naked and restrained with cable ties. A suspect believed to have been the victim’s boyfriend was arrested and remains in custody.
Few of the victims have been formally identified.
Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo went missing last week on her daily afternoon jog and the 38-year-old’s naked body was found behind a hotel in Kempton Park several days later.
Police have offered a R400,000 (£18,400) reward for any information that could lead to the arrest of the killer or killers, while the Democratic Alliance, the second-largest political party in South Africa, has offered R500,000.
The latest national crime figures show that between April and June, an average of nearly 60 people each day were murdered in the country.
Cyril Ramaphosa, the president, has declared violence against women to be a national crisis.
South Africa has some of the world’s highest levels of gender-based violence, with the rate at which women are killed being five times higher than the global average, according to UN Women.
summary: Residents near Johannesburg fear a serial killer may be operating after the ninth body of a young woman was discovered in the Ekurhuleni municipality. Police have not yet confirmed if the deaths are connected, though they acknowledge concerning similarities in the cases. Authorities have intensified investigations, set up checkpoints, and offered substantial rewards for information leading to arrests.
key_points: Nine bodies of young women aged 20 to 38 have been found in the Ekurhuleni municipality east of Johannesburg.
The latest unidentified victim, approximately 30 years old, was found with her throat cut and a stab wound.
South African police have not officially confirmed whether the deaths are linked to a serial killer.
Authorities have set up checkpoints, plan to lock down Kempton Park, and are comparing evidence across cases.
Police and the Democratic Alliance have offered a combined total of R900,000 in rewards for information.

title: Metsola: Australia, New Zealand could be next EU 'associated members'
author: Maria Tadeo; Vincenzo Genovese
content:
Metsola tells Euronews pitch for “associate membership” with Canada will strengthen cooperation with like-minded countries and incite new ones.
European Parliament President Roberta Metsola has told Euronews that countries including Australia and New Zealand could follow Canada in becoming “associate members” of the European Union as like-minded nations seek closer ties.
Speaking exclusively to Europe Today ahead of a speech by Canadian Prime MInister Mark Carny on Thursday_,_ Metsola described the proposed status as a third way between full EU membership and candidate status.
“There are countries with which we want to deepen our relationship,” Metsola said.
"I don't doubt that it will include other countries, and others will come knocking at our door...In such times of uncertainty, having friends matters."
The EU already has trade agreements with both countries, providing a potential starting point for closer cooperation. A similar relationship has been proposed with Canada, which signed a comprehensive trade agreement with the EU in 2016.
Asked about the technicalities of what associate membership would look like, Metsola acknowledged that talks are still at an early stage, while pointing to deeper trade relations, access to critical raw materials and common regulations on issues that “like-minded” countries care deeply about, such as social media and the protection of minors.
On Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed “associate membership” for Canada in her annual State of the Union address.
Canadian Prime Minister Carney is exploring closer ties with the bloc amid a trade war with the US, Canada’s biggest trading partner, with prohibitive tariffs in place. Under pressure from President Donald Trump, Ottawa is rethinking its place in the world, while Carney has been vocal in calling for an alliance of “middle powers”.
No reason for retaliation
After the announcement, Trump told reporters he would consider imposing fresh tariffs on the European Union if the bid for associate membership turns "hostile".
Washington and Brussels have a trade deal in place, under which the EU faces a 15% tariff on goods.
Metsola played down the threats, saying the EU views its relationships with the two countries separately. She said that the EU does not work against anyone but acts as an advocate for rules-based cooperation.
She also pointed to the trade deal agreed last summer and ratified this year.
Separately, a spokesperson for the European Commission said: “The proposed strengthening of our partnership is not against anyone, but for our common strength.”
Carney is due to address the European Parliament on Thursday at 11.30am.
Peggy Corlin contributed to reporting.
summary: European Parliament President Roberta Metsola stated that countries like Australia and New Zealand could follow Canada in pursuing a new 'associate membership' status with the European Union. This proposed tier between full membership and candidate status aims to deepen cooperation on trade, critical raw materials, and common regulations among like-minded nations. While U.S. President Donald Trump threatened potential tariffs on the EU if the Canadian bid becomes hostile, EU officials have downplayed the threats, emphasizing that the partnerships are not directed against any other country.
key_points: Australia and New Zealand could potentially become EU 'associate members,' following a proposal initially made for Canada.
Associate membership offers a third way between full EU membership and candidate status, focusing on trade, raw materials, and shared regulations.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is exploring closer ties with the EU amid ongoing trade tensions with the United States.
U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to impose fresh tariffs on the EU if Canada's bid for associate membership turns hostile.
EU officials dismissed Trump's threats, stating that the strengthened partnerships aim to promote rules-based cooperation rather than oppose other nations.

title: Canada becoming EU âassociate memberâ would be positive move, Carney says
author: Live Reporting Edited by Alex Smith; Manish Pandey; With Robin Levinson King
content:
![Pierre Poilievre, leader of Canada's Conservative Party, pictured in April 2026.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/640/cpsprodpb/vivo/live/images/2026/9/17/9aa7c726-38fb-463a-b782-9fa60573772a.jpg.webp) Image source, Getty Images
While Prime Minister Mark Carney and key leaders in Europe appear to be in lockstep, some opposition politicians in Canada are critical of the prospect of becoming an EU "associate member".
Speaking before Carney's speech to the European Parliament, Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre says decisions for the country "must not be made in Washington, Beijing, or Brussels".
Poilievre voices his disapproval of a possible associate membership, or "unique alliance", saying that while Conservatives support free trade, and Nato co-operation with European allies, they reject any prospects of EU taxes, laws and open-border rules on immigration in Canada.
Meanwhile Adam Chambers, MP for Simcoe North in Ontario, told BBC News ahead of Carney's speech "it could be a concrete, meaningful proposal. Or it could be just words and vibes".
Chambers alluded to the existing Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement trade deal between the EU and Canada, highlighting that it is still waiting for ratification by multiple EU countries.
summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney's potential move toward Canada becoming an EU "associate member" has drawn mixed reactions. While European leaders and Carney appear aligned, Canadian Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre strongly opposes the idea, rejecting EU taxes, laws, and open borders. Other opposition figures, like MP Adam Chambers, question whether the proposal is substantive or merely rhetorical given that the existing Canada-EU trade deal awaits full ratification.
key_points: Mark Carney faces criticism from Canadian opposition politicians over the prospect of Canada becoming an EU associate member.
Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre rejected EU laws, taxes, and open-border immigration rules for Canada.
Poilievre stated that decisions for Canada must not be made in Washington, Beijing, or Brussels.
MP Adam Chambers questioned if the proposal is meaningful or just "words and vibes," noting that the existing CETA trade deal still awaits ratification by multiple EU nations.

title: Photos show charred wreckage from deadly crash of news helicopter in LA
author: Sareen Habeshian
content:
![The National Transportation Safety Board released photos of the aftermath of the Los Angeles helicopter crash that killed three people.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/269b/live/b04f79b0-b212-11f1-95f2-19e1a2e8eef2.jpg)
- Published
Investigators have released new photos that show the stark aftermath of a news helicopter crash that killed three people in Los Angeles on Tuesday night.
A scorched aircraft and charred storage container were being examined at the scene of the incident on Wednesday. The collision claimed the lives of NBC photojournalist Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw.
The third victim, a pedestrian, was identified as Edy Gutierrez Mejia, 29, by the coroner's office.
The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), which is leading the investigation into the incident, said a report on the cause could take up to 18 months.
![The National Transportation Safety Board released photos of the aftermath of the Los Angeles helicopter crash that killed three people.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/7c66/live/daeac350-b212-11f1-95f2-19e1a2e8eef2.jpg)
NBC Los Angeles said its NewsChopper4, which also operated for the Spanish-language Telemundo 52, was in the city's suburb on Tuesday night reporting on a deadly bus crash that had killed two people.
Several other news helicopters were also overhead in the area.
The driver in the bus crash has since been arrested on suspicion of murder.
The cause of the aircraft crash has not yet been determined, officials said. Marciniw was reportedly an experienced pilot.
Mejia, the pedestrian killed when the helicopter came down, was a Guatemalan national who had only arrived in Los Angeles this week, according to NBC News.
Moment NBC anchors confirm their helicopter crash
Investigators were collecting data at the crash site on Wednesday. The helicopter will be moved to a secure facility, where the NTSB will continue to examine the wreckage.
The NTSB is an independent US government agency that investigates civil transportation accidents.
During a news conference on Wednesday, the NTSB's investigator-in-charge Fabian Salazar said a preliminary report on the incident would be issued within 30 days.
A final report on the cause of the crash could take up to 18 months to be released, he added.
Asked by reporters about video circulating on social media that appears to show the helicopter's viewpoint in the seconds before the crash, Salazar said it is so far "probably the most important evidence" for investigators.
![Photojournalist Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw are hown taking a selfie. She is wearing a black puffy jacket and smiling and he is wearing a black puffy vest and smiling. They are standing in front of a helipcopter on the ground](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/157d/live/78f7ac60-b219-11f1-a430-4d16ee157c41.jpg)
Photojournalist Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw
In addition to the three people killed, two others were taken to the hospital.
During emotional live coverage on NBC4 on Tuesday night, veteran news anchor Colleen Williams confirmed it was the local news station's helicopter that crashed.
While news coverage via helicopter is not necessarily unique to Los Angeles, it is more prominent compared to other major metropolitan areas.
LA local news stations regularly break into live programming to broadcast high-speed police pursuits from the air, fly over wildfires and show accidents, protests, and holiday traffic jams in often unscripted, real-time aerials.
![Graphic showing the locations of two crash sites in the Chatsworth area of Los Angeles, California. An aerial map marks a bus crash on the junction of De Soto Avenue and Nordhoff Street and a helicopter crash just over 600 metres to the north east in an industrial area. An inset map shows Chatsworth's location within Los Angeles, with a second inset highlighting Californiaâs location in the south west of the US.Â](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/6db0/live/a8cf4b00-b219-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.jpg)
summary: The National Transportation Safety Board has released new photos showing the charred wreckage of a news helicopter that crashed in Los Angeles on Tuesday night, killing three people. The crash claimed the lives of NBC photojournalist Eliana Moreno, pilot George Marciniw, and a pedestrian named Edy Gutierrez Mejia. Investigators stated that a preliminary report will be issued within 30 days, while a final report on the cause of the crash could take up to 18 months.
key_points: Three people were killed in the Los Angeles news helicopter crash, including photojournalist Eliana Moreno, pilot George Marciniw, and pedestrian Edy Gutierrez Mejia.
The helicopter, belonging to NBC Los Angeles, was in the area reporting on an earlier deadly bus crash.
Two other individuals were taken to the hospital following the incident.
The NTSB stated that a preliminary report will be released within 30 days, with a final determination taking up to 18 months.
Investigators are currently reviewing a video circulating on social media that shows the helicopter's viewpoint before the crash as key evidence.

title: Trump calls EU offer to Canada of associate membership ‘laughable’, while threatening tariffs
author: Agencies; Guardian staff reporter
content:
Donald Trump has threatened the European Union with “serious tariffs” and a cut to trade after the bloc proposed to make Canada its first ever associate member, calling the idea “laughable”.
Suggesting the move was a “hostile act”, the US president told reporters he could put “very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe”. He added: “If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe.”
European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen invited Canada to become the EU’s first “associate member” on Wednesday, a day before Canadian prime minister Mark Carney was due to address the European parliament.
Von der Leyen pitched closer cooperation on tech, defence and energy to Carney, telling the European parliament that, as democracies face a “fracture in the international rules-based system”, Brussels and Ottawa needed to pull closer together.
Canada and the EU already have a trade deal and numerous bilateral agreements, but have been moving closer since Donald Trump returned to the White House and raised tariffs on both old allies, while repeatedly talking about Canada becoming the 51st US state and lambasting the EU.
In a sign that Canada was seeking to further diversify its defence ties away from the United States, Carney’s office announced on Wednesday that the country had formally applied to join the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force military coalition.
The force is a rapid response military partnership comprised of 10 North Atlantic Nato member states, including Denmark, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden.
On Wednesday, Carney and British prime minister Andy Burnham held a bilateral meeting at the grounds of Everton football club. The leaders, who are both fans of the premiership club, then attended the team’s game against Wolves.
![Mark Carney and Andy Burnham pose for a picture ahead of an Everton match on Wednesday evening.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/adef16397480429a8b3241ecd61bed4f47aec358/0_0_2000_1362/master/2000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The two discussed deepening defence cooperation and the opportunities and challenges presented by artificial intelligence. Downing Street said both prime ministers emphasised the importance of building close ties with European partners, particularly on trade and defence.
The 27-member EU has never had an associate membership category, although it has close ties with Norway, Iceland and Switzerland, allowing deep economic integration with these countries, who follow many EU rules. However it remains to be seen what associate membership means, including for Canada’s relationship with the EU single market.
Von der Leyen said on Wednesday it was time to move from cooperation based on trade to a broader “alliance for the future” and “bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible.
“We will work on intelligent manufacturing. We will create a tech alliance. We will integrate defence industrial bases. We will make the Arctic a flagship joint project,” she said.
She listed energy, critical minerals, batteries, AI, cyber and economic security as other fields of cooperation. “This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” she said.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters
summary: US President Donald Trump threatened the European Union with serious tariffs and halted trade after the bloc proposed making Canada its first associate member. European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen pitched closer cooperation on tech, defence, and energy to Canadian prime minister Mark Carney. Meanwhile, Canada has formally applied to join the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force military coalition to diversify its defence ties away from the United States.
key_points: Donald Trump called the EU's offer of associate membership to Canada 'laughable' and threatened serious tariffs on Europe.
Ursula von der Leyen invited Canada to become the EU's first associate member to foster closer cooperation in tech, defence, and energy.
Canada formally applied to join the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force military coalition.
Canadian prime minister Mark Carney met with British prime minister Andy Burnham to discuss defence cooperation and artificial intelligence.

title: Audio captures tragic final moments of NBC News helicopter before fatal crash
author: Shweta Sharma
content:
Three people have been killed after an NBC News helicopter crashed in Los Angeles, with audio capturing the chilling moment a voice onboard asks the pilot: “What? You can’t pull up?”
NBC4 Los Angeles identified two of the victims as pilot George Marciniw and aerial photojournalist Eliana Moreno, a familiar face to viewers of the network and its Spanish-language sister station, Telemundo 52. The third person, who was on the ground at the time of the crash, has yet to be named.
The helicopter was on the scene in Chatsworth in the San Fernando Valley Tuesday to film the aftermath of a traffic accident, which saw a city bus collide with an SUV earlier in the day, leaving two dead and six injured.
Hovering nearby, the chopper was filming the wreckage of the bus smash, meaning live video transmissions were being sent back to its parent TV station for review when it suddenly got into difficulties.
The aircraft crashed between two commercial buildings, a Los Angeles Fire Department spokesperson said later, with three people pronounced dead at the scene and another transported to a local hospital. Their condition is currently unknown.
![Eliana Moreno and George Marciniw have been named as two of the people killed](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/16/8/23/Screenshot-2026-09-16-at-09-37-07.png)
Veteran chopper pilot and former Emmy-winning news reporter Zoey Tur, famed for filming the OJ Simpson Bronco chase, posted a clip of footage on X.
“If you listen, you could hear the low rotor RPM annunciator horn going off,” the expert wrote.
“You could also hear the engine rev down. This was an engine failure, and slow response into entering an auto-rotation by PiC [Pilot in Command].”
NBC Los Angeles and Telemundo 52 issued a joint statement paying tribute to Marciniw and Moreno, who both hailed from Southern California.
“We are deeply saddened to share that a helicopter providing aerial news coverage for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 was involved in a fatal accident in Los Angeles on Tuesday evening,” the statement said. “We extend our heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives.”
Before the victims were identified, NBC4 had reported live on air that it was its own helicopter, NewsChopper 4, that had crashed.
“We’ve been telling you that we’ve been piecing it together here,” NBC anchor Colleen Williams said.
“We knew it was a news chopper. We knew we’d lost contact with our people out there, and we’ve just received the confirmation that, in fact, NewsChopper 4 went down just before 7 o’clock tonight in Chatsworth.”
Footage from the resulting scene showed at least four vehicles and two shipping containers burning and firefighters working to extinguish the blaze. Seventy firefighters ultimately descended on the scene and succeeded in putting it out.
The Los Angeles Police Department later put the exact time of the crash at 6:58 p.m. and said its officers had responded to the area of Lurline Avenue and Nordhoff Street.
The other person killed in the crash was outside in a parking lot next to the commercial building, said LAFD spokesman Captain Branden Silverman at a news conference. They have not yet been identified.
Eyewitness Zareh Sevanesian told NBC he had been driving nearby when he noticed the chopper’s erratic descent.
“As we were driving I looked over to my left,” he said. “I saw the helicopter – something didn’t look right. And I told my wife, ‘That helicopter is not flying right.’”
![Tributes have been paid to photojournalist Moreno](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/16/8/25/Eliana-Moreno54231-e2a43ba9.jpeg)
When it came down, Sevanesian said he pulled up at the crash site, describing the inferno he encountered as “one of the most violent fires I had ever seen.”
He said he found a person near the wreckage and three more screaming, with his wife Allyona Sevanesian adding: “It was very terrifying and sad for everyone.”
Reflecting on the tragedy early Wednesday, NBC4 reporter Lauren Coronado said: “I think a lot of us are still trying to process what happened, this terrible loss.” She was standing near the crash site during her newscast and said a hazmat crew was on site cleaning up jet fuel.
In a tribute to Moreno and Marciniw, her newscast referred to them as ”the team in the sky,” saying Moreno would often post videos from her job and was in awe of the view she had.
News anchor Lynette Romero held a colleague’s hand and wiped away tears after hearing Moreno’s voice when one of her posts was played.
In an interview with the station, Esteban Jimenez, a pilot, said he had known Marciniw since the 1990s. He said Marciniw had been his instructor. “I just talked to him on Sunday. We were talking about the aviation business and retiring,” he said.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said she was “absolutely devastated” by the loss of life in the twin disasters Tuesday.
“My heart is with the families and loved ones of those we lost in the tragic bus collision and helicopter crash,” she said, going on to thank emergency responders for their swift response.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom also shared his condolences and said: “Our hearts are with the victims and families of tonight’s devastating Metro bus and helicopter crashes in Chatsworth, and with the entire NBC4 family.”
The National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration will investigate the chopper crash, the fire department said, but have so refused to be drawn on what might have caused it.
summary: An NBC News helicopter crashed in the Chatsworth area of Los Angeles while filming the aftermath of a traffic accident, resulting in three deaths. The victims identified include pilot George Marciniw and photojournalist Eliana Moreno, alongside a third unidentified person on the ground. Audio from the aircraft captured a voice asking the pilot why he could not pull up before the crash between two commercial buildings. Local officials, including Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass and California Governor Gavin Newsom, expressed their condolences while the NTSB and FAA investigate the incident.
key_points: Three people were killed when an NBC News helicopter crashed in Chatsworth, Los Angeles.
The victims identified so far are pilot George Marciniw and aerial photojournalist Eliana Moreno, with a third ground victim yet to be named.
The helicopter was filming the aftermath of an earlier traffic accident involving a city bus and an SUV when it experienced difficulties.
Audio from the flight captured a voice asking the pilot, 'What? You can't pull up?'
The NTSB and FAA will investigate the cause of the fatal crash.

title: Brussels won’t offer ‘associate EU membership’ to Brexit Britain
author: Jon Stone; Gabriel Gavin; Emilio Casalicchio; Sam Blewett
content:
LONDON — The European Union has just offered Canada “associate EU membership.” Don’t expect it to do the same for Brexit Britain.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s surprise announcement came during her State of the Union address in Strasbourg on Wednesday.
“We share one ocean, one set of values, one way of seeing the world,” she said, inviting Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to help make his country “the first associate member of the European Union.”
summary: During her State of the Union address, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen surprised observers by inviting Canada to become the first 'associate member' of the European Union. Von der Leyen highlighted shared values and a common ocean as the basis for this unprecedented offer. However, reports indicate that the EU will not extend this same associate membership opportunity to Brexit Britain.
key_points: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen offered Canada associate EU membership during her State of the Union address.
Von der Leyen cited shared values and seeing the world the same way as reasons for the Canadian invitation.
The article notes that Brexit Britain should not expect to receive a similar offer of associate EU membership.

title: NBC helicopter crash in LA kills at least three people with others injured
author: The Associated Press; Guardian staff reporter
content:
A news helicopter crash in a Los Angeles neighborhood has killed at least three people, after it came to the ground and burst into flames near the site of a bus crash that occurred hours earlier.
The helicopter crashed near a one-storey commercial building in the neighborhood of Chatsworth in the San Fernando Valley, as news crews were covering the bus crash that left at least two people dead and six others injured, according the Los Angeles Fire Department.
An NBC4 Los Angeles anchor at the station confirmed during a live broadcast that its chopper went down just before 7pm.
At least one person killed in the helicopter crash was outside in the parking lot next to the commercial building, Capt Branden Silverman, a spokesperson for the Los Angeles Fire Department, said during a news conference. It was unclear if the other two who were killed were on the ground or inside the aircraft.
One person was taken to the hospital, but their condition was not immediately clear.
![Investigators work the scene after the helicopter crashed near a bus crash in Chatsworth, a neighborhood in Los Angeles, Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/df7efd7d25866af8232045e69d7eaee76dd57b01/0_0_4200_2800/master/4200.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
“We’re trying to determine how many patients were inside the helicopter,” said Silverman, who described the helicopter as “pretty well destroyed” and adding that officials would be sorting through the rubble to see how many victims were on board.
At least four cars and two storage containers on the ground burned after the helicopter caught fire, which was quickly put out, according to officials. More than 50 firefighters responded to the helicopter crash, according to the fire department.
About two hours before the crash, an SUV slammed into the middle of a city bus, killing at least two people and injuring six others. Photos and videos online showed half of the SUV lodged into the side of an MTA bus.
The helicopter crashed about a 1.5 miles from the bus crash.
The National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration said it will be investigating the cause of the helicopter crash.
summary: An NBC4 news helicopter covering a fatal bus crash in the Chatsworth neighborhood of Los Angeles went down and burst into flames, killing at least three people. The crash occurred near a commercial building, damaging multiple cars and storage containers while leaving the aircraft severely destroyed. Authorities and federal agencies, including the NTSB and FAA, are investigating the incident.
key_points: A news helicopter crashed in the Chatsworth neighborhood of Los Angeles, resulting in at least three deaths.
The helicopter was covering an earlier bus crash that had killed two people and injured six others.
At least one fatality occurred in the parking lot outside a commercial building where the helicopter went down.
The crash sparked a fire that burned four cars and two storage containers before being extinguished by over 50 firefighters.
The NTSB and FAA are investigating the cause of the helicopter crash.

title: EU chief backs plan for Canada to become 'associate member'
author: Amy Walker; Nick Beake
content:
![A smiling Mark Carney, wearing a suit, walks alongside European Parliament President Roberta Metsola and Ursula von der Leyen at the European Parliament](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/b431/live/3960b020-b1b9-11f1-bdcf-d393eb724fa3.jpg)
Mark Carney (left) walks alongside European Parliament President Roberta Metsola (centre) and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen (right)
- Published
The president of the European Commission has backed proposals for Canada to become the EU's first "associate member".
Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament on Wednesday she wanted to work on "opening the door" for Canada, which would involve closer ties on various key sectors.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney last week spoke of seeking a "unique alliance" with the EU. The country currently faces tense relations with the US, compounded by an intensifying dispute over trade.
Without mentioning US President Donald Trump by name, von der Leyen said offering Canada some sort of EU membership was "not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strength".
She added: "Partnerships are a strategic choice for Europe. But they also respond to the fracture in the international rules-based system".
Carney was in attendance at the annual key note speech in Strasbourg, and is due to address the parliament on Thursday.
Trade talks between Canada and the US collapsed last month, sparking a series of new tariff measures. Trump's repeated talk of making Canada a "51st state" has also helped to fuel the feud between the North American neighbours.
Von der Leyen told the EU's State of the Union address that the bloc and Canada "see the world with the same eyes", including on topics ranging from AI, to climate change and geopolitics.
"And we have stood together: on Ukraine, on defence, on raw materials and on supply chains. But above all... Europe and Canada believe in democracy."
She did not give specific details on how any Canadian membership would work, but listed manufacturing, technology, AI, defence, energy, critical minerals and economic security as key areas for cooperation.
![Ursula von der Leyen, who has a grey/blonde short haircut, wears a cream blazer and blouse as she speaks at a podium, with the EU flag in the background](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/2366/live/12ba6710-b1bc-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.jpg)
Von der Leyen said it was time to bring the EU's relationship with Canada to "the highest level possible"
Both she and other European leaders have found a reliable ally in Carney as they deal with similar problems.
In particular, they have faced Trump's aggressive use of tariffs and his threat to annex Greenland which is a sovereign territory of EU member Denmark.
But "associate membership" of the EU does not currently exist and the process, if agreed, could take years.
Earlier this year, Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz suggested - to a mixed reaction - that Ukraine could be granted this new status.
Some countries in the western Balkans including Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, and Serbia are already on the long road towards full EU membership.
In Eastern Europe, Georgia and Moldova are also applying.
Ten of the bloc's 27 members are yet to ratify a free-trade agreement struck with Ottawa nearly a decade ago, and some capitals would prefer to build on existing defence and trade agreements rather than create a new form of membership for Canada.
Setting out the EU's political and policy priorities for year ahead, von der Leyen also proposed the formation of a European Security Council, which would include the UK and Ukraine, amid an ongoing threat to the continent from Russia.
"For a long time, we have discussed a leaders' format focused on the security of our continent, with partners like Canada, Norway, Ukraine, the United Kingdom and others involved," she said in the wide-ranging address.
"This is even more urgent now, given the nature and scale of the risks at play. This is why we will set out our ideas to make a European Security Council a reality."
Alongside global threats, von der Leyen also said many European families were worried about the cost of living, and the "dizzying speed of change" of technology and its impacts on jobs and society.
Other proposals included inviting the world's largest AI labs for talks on how to support industry efforts to pace the frontier, as well as slashing bureaucracy for businesses in the EU.
A new emergency tool to help countries better deal with mass migration movements following the deadly influx of migrants to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in July would also be outlined.
Plans to curb social media use among children, including banning platforms for under 13s, were also put forward. Under the proposal, children aged 13 to 15 would only be able to set up social media accounts which are supervised by parents.
  - Published9 January
 ![Trump on the left, Starmer and Macron on the right](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/cdd1/live/eb492840-ec7e-11f0-b385-5f48925de19a.jpg)
- ![Mark Carney, in a black suit and tie gestures as he stands in front of a microphone. Behind him, against a dark background, are three red and white Canadian flags in a row.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/b067/live/866137e0-adff-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.jpg)
summary: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has backed proposals for Canada to become the EU's first associate member to foster closer ties in sectors like AI, defence, and critical minerals. The move comes amid strained trade relations and disputes between Canada and the United States. However, associate membership does not currently exist as a status, and creating it could take years.
key_points: Ursula von der Leyen voiced support for opening the door for Canada to become an EU associate member.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney previously sought a unique alliance with the EU amid tense trade relations with the US.
Potential cooperation areas include manufacturing, technology, AI, defence, energy, and critical minerals.
Associate membership does not currently exist, and establishing it could take years with potential resistance from some EU capitals.

title: Three dead in Los Angeles news helicopter crash
author: Sareen Habeshian
content:
Smoke and flames rise from Los Angeles fatal helicopter crash site
- Published
Three people have died and two others taken to hospital after a news helicopter crashed in suburban Los Angeles, fire authorities in the city have said.
NBC Los Angeles confirmed the helicopter was its NewsChopper4, which also operated for Telemundo 52, and was in the area on Tuesday reporting on a deadly bus crash.
The aircraft went down just before 19:00 local time (01:00 BST) between two commercial buildings in the Chatsworth neighbourhood, a Los Angeles Fire Department (LAFD) spokesperson told the BBC.
The Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) said it was not yet known how many people were onboard, and no victim names had been released.
Fire from the crash spread to four vehicles and two storage containers, and more than 70 firefighters were deployed to the scene, the LAFD said.
During emotional live coverage on NBC4, veteran news anchor Colleen Williams confirmed it was the local news station's helicopter that crashed.
"We knew it was a news chopper. We knew we'd lost contact with our people out there, and we've just received confirmation," Williams said.
Earlier, LAFD Captain Branden Silverman told the local affiliate of the BBC's US partner CBS: "We do have one confirmed patient that seemed to be outside of the helicopter when it crashed.
"That person was declared deceased on scene," Silverman said.
Several news helicopters were in the area at the time of the incident reporting on a bus crash.
Earlier in the day, two people were killed and six others were injured after an SUV crashed into a city bus in Chatsworth, BBC's US partner CBS reported.
![A vehicle appears to be on fire next to shipping containers. Smoke is billowing from the containers.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/4110/live/03c9e4a0-b17c-11f1-a430-4d16ee157c41.jpg)
LAPD's Central Division posted on X that it extended "thoughts and prayers to the family, friends and colleagues of KNBC 4, Los Angeles".
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass wrote on X she was "absolutely devastated by the loss of life in Chatsworth tonight".
"My heart is with the families and loved ones of those we lost in the tragic bus collision and helicopter crash," she added.
California Governor Gavin Newsom wrote on X that "our hearts are with the victims and families of tonight's devastating Metro bus and helicopter crashes in Chatsworth, and with the entire NBC4 family".
"Thank you to the first responders working tirelessly tonight."
The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) will lead the investigation into the incident.
summary: Three people died and two others were hospitalized after an NBC Los Angeles news helicopter crashed in the Chatsworth neighbourhood. The aircraft, identified as NewsChopper4, went down between two commercial buildings while in the area reporting on an earlier deadly bus crash. More than 70 firefighters responded to the scene as the crash sparked fires affecting vehicles and storage containers.
key_points: Three people died and two were taken to the hospital in the crash.
The downed aircraft was NBC Los Angeles's NewsChopper4, which also operated for Telemundo 52.
The crash occurred just before 19:00 local time in the Chatsworth neighbourhood between two commercial buildings.
The helicopter was in the area reporting on an earlier fatal bus crash.
The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) will lead the investigation into the incident.

title: NATO jet shoots down suspected Russian drone over Lithuania
author: Al Jazeera Staff
content:
![U.S. Air Force A-10 Thunderbolt aircrafts fly during the U.S. led Saber Strike exercise in the air over Latvia June 6, 2018. REUTERS/Ints Kalnins](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/2018-06-06T133139Z_447411981_RC15C9ECF920_RTRMADP_3_NATO-RUSSIA-EXERCISE-1789006576.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
An Italian fighter jet flying for NATO has brought down what officials said was a suspected Russian drone in Lithuanian airspace.
According to Lithuania’s national crisis management centre, the drone entered the country’s airspace on Tuesday from Belarus and was shot down near the small settlement of Pratkunai in central Lithuania, just north of the country’s second-largest city, Kaunas.
Recommended Stories
